Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

info.title: TuneTwins: An Intrinsically Motivating Game Paradigm for Scalable Music Cognition Research

text.text: Researchers across the behavioral sciences are increasingly using games as a means of data collection.
Intrinsically motivating digital games are especially promising for music cognition, where large, diverse, and engaged samples are needed.
In this article, we focus on a specific class of game paradigms suited to cross-cultural contexts and applicable across the developmental lifespan: auditory matching-pairs (Memory) games.
We present the conception, design, and initial evaluation of TuneTwins, a solitaire auditory matching-pairs paradigm developed to study musical memory and auditory cognition.
Building on self-determination theory and prior game-based research, TuneTwins employs an 8-pair (4 × 4) board to balance playability with psychometric sensitivity.

Our web-based auditory adaptation introduces clear visual-auditory mappings, a three-click turn structure, and a dual scoring system that distinguishes memorized matches from lucky guesses and memory errors.

Large-scale simulations of chance and optimal strategies guided the choice of board size, demonstrating that this configuration yields meaningful separation between performance extremes while avoiding ceiling effects.

We further report empirical evidence from four implementations: a proof-of-concept online study, a cross-cultural field study with Mbendjele BaYaka hunter-gatherers, a study with visitors to a science museum, and an online global deployment.

In the proof-of-concept study, TuneTwins captured systematic performance differences between stimulus conditions; across all settings, it elicited high voluntary engagement, including repeated play and the completion of multiple difficulty levels.

We argue that matching-pairs games such as TuneTwins provide an engaging, intuitive, and scalable paradigm for collecting behavioral data using primarily auditory stimuli-and that they can be used to probe the mental representation of music across cultures, across development, and potentially across species.

text.text: Beyond standardization, the experimental procedure itself exerts a substantial influence on data quality.
Specifically, the extent to which participants are genuinely engaged in the task critically determines whether the collected data capture and reflect the underlying cognitive processes.

As web-based experimentation has become increasingly prevalent in cognitive and psychological research-especially during the COVID-19 pandemic-crowdsourcing platforms such as MTurk and Prolific, which provide access to large participant pools, have accordingly become primary vehicles for scaling up data collection (Stewart et al., 2017).

text.text: However, although material incentives such as monetary rewards may increase the duration or frequency of participation, this form of extrinsic motivation typically frames the experiment as a means to an external reward rather than as an activity experienced as valuable in itself.

This framing can readily result in superficial or random responses and ultimately compromise data quality (Hauser et al., 2019), particularly given that many cognitive experiments are experienced by participants as "effortful, frustrating, and repetitive" (Lumsden et al., 2016, para. 1).

text.text: Moreover, MTurk and similar platforms have experienced declining rates of population replenishment and increasing participant non-naïveté.

The participant pools on these platforms are relatively small, demographically narrow, and highly experienced, with many individuals having completed hundreds of similar tasks (Chmielewski & Kucker, 2020; Stewart et al., 2017).

text.text: As more researchers draw repeatedly from the same pool of experienced participants, that pool becomes progressively less naïve and less representative, ultimately diminishing its value as a scientific resource.
To address this persistent challenge of collecting high-quality data, one solution is to make participation intrinsically enjoyable and engaging.
When players are immersed in a game and motivated by intrinsic satisfaction, the resulting gameplay traces are more likely to faithfully reflect their perceptual and cognitive processes.

Over three decades of research have shown that the quality of experience and performance differs substantially depending on whether behavior is driven by intrinsic or extrinsic motivation (Deci & Ryan, 1985; Lepper et al., 1973; Ryan & Deci, 2000).

For example, the Hooked on Music paradigm collected data from over 200,000 unpaid participants (Burgoyne et al., 2013), the Clapping Music app was downloaded more than 140,000 times within three years (Duffy & Pearce, 2018), and comparable large-scale participation effects have been reported in other studies (Tiago et al., 2017).

text.text: Better yet, the game is not only fun but also intuitive-an essential feature for collecting data across diverse cultural contexts.

With the majority of music psychology research conducted on WEIRD participants (Henrich et al., 2010), often using Western music, we risk viewing the human mechanisms underlying music perception and production through a narrow lens.

text.text: Repeatedly focusing on a narrow subset of the world's musical and cultural diversity risks illuminating only one corner of a much larger phenomenon.
As a result, key scientific questions concerning the origins of music and the balance between cultural variability and universality remain difficult to address.

A necessary step toward a more comprehensive understanding is the development of cross-cultural studies supported by carefully designed experimental procedures that are intuitive, accessible, and applicable across diverse cultural settings.

As Jacoby et al. (2020) remind us in their position paper, cross-cultural study faces challenges of "potential lack of conceptual common ground between researcher and participants, a factor that might lead to mistranslations, misunderstanding, and the absence of explicit, formalized terms for core research concepts " (p. 191).

text.text: Imagine investing considerable time and effort into designing a perfect experiment-one that is both highly engaging and capable of measuring the target theoretical construct-only to find, upon implementing it in an entirely unfamiliar culture, that there is no reliable way to convey its rules and instructions.
We argue that intuitiveness is a key factor in enhancing the cross-cultural scalability of experimental paradigms.
Because language is deeply embedded in cultural practices, tasks that rely on verbal instructions risk introducing unintended cultural biases or differences in comprehension.
Reducing linguistic demands is therefore advisable when designing paradigms intended for crosscultural use.
Nonverbal forms of communication-such as demonstration-tend to be more universally understood.
An intuitive paradigm that is self-explanatory or easy to demonstrate thus reduces the danger of misinterpretation inherent in verbal instructions alone.

Together, these considerations underscore a central challenge in music-cognition research: collecting data from diverse and meaningfully engaged participants while relying on experimental paradigms that are both robust and scalable.
We propose that one solution to meet this goal is to foster intrinsic motivation through intuitive gamified experiments-in other words, science games.

This paper presents the design, characteristics, and underlying logic structure of a novel music science game, TuneTwins (i.e., an auditory matching-pairs game), along with simulations designed to examine its capability to capture the distribution of participants' performance.
We also report evidence bearing on participants' motivation to complete the game.

We further argue that paradigm design is not merely a matter of translating a theoretical construct into a task; rather, the upstream process of conceptualization, game experience design, and formal evaluation-while distinct from empirical data collection-is essential for ensuring validity and scalability, yet is often overlooked in cognitive research.

This neglect is compounded by a practical bottleneck: the infrastructural demands of developing and deploying game-like research platforms, including interface design, stimulus management, online deployment, and data recording pipelines.
Although the scientific value of such approaches is increasingly recognized (Long et al., 2023), these demands continue to deter adoption.

text.text: The design of TuneTwins was informed by both of these considerations.

text.text: Musical memory is a particularly meaningful research subject for cross-cultural research as memory is a fundamental, biologically grounded cognitive capacity shared across human populations.

Evidence suggests that memory performance for music does not strongly depend on formal music training-naïve listeners often perform comparably to trained musicians when the material is familiar (Bigand & Poulin-Charronnat, 2006; Levitin, 1994; Levitin & Cook, 1996).

The appeal of the Memory game can be attributed to several psychological factors.

First, the task directly challenges memory and reflects participants' cognitive processes through their card choices (e.g., when they have already listened to two cards that belong to a pair, do they remember to match them?).

Second, because it is a children's game played in cultures around the world, its rules of play are exceptionally simple and intuitive, allowing players of various age groups and cultural backgrounds to engage without extensive instruction needed.
Third, the Memory game satisfies a basic cognitive drive for problem-solving and self-improvement (Ryan & Deci, 2000) by challenging players to memorize and match pairs to win.

text.text: The game also provides immediate feedback-each attempt yields either a successful match or an error-which sustains attention and fosters intrinsic motivation through trial-and-error learning (Malone, 1981).

text.text: Finally, Memory offers both individual challenges and multiplayer competition, making it versatile as a solitary or interactive activity.
These features not only explain its enduring popularity but also highlight its potential as a robust paradigm for experimental adaptation.

text.text: Collectively, these studies provide strong evidence of the potential of the matching-pairs paradigm.
In a typical Memory game, players are presented with a board with 𝑛 pairs of cards.
Taking turns, players flip two cards at a time.
If the two flipped cards are identical, they constitute a pair, and the pair is collected by the player (removed from the board) as a point.
If the two flipped cards are different, the cards are flipped back and no point is awarded (or point deducted depending on the scoring rule).
The game ends when the board is cleared, and the player who matched most pairs is the winner.
Although it is typically played with two players, the game can also be played in solitaire.
In a solitaire version, the goal of the game is to clear the board with as few turns as possible, with fewer turns indicating better performance.
The optimal strategy for both the two-player version (Zwick & Paterson, 1993) and the solitaire version (Foerster & Wattenhofer, 2013) have been discussed and analyzed in detail.

text.text: According to Zwick and Paterson, two-player gameplay involves the use of optimal strategies that increase a player's chance of winning in competitive settings.
However, certain strategies intended to hinder the opponent can distort the measurement of memory performance in experimental data.

One such behavior is the idling strategy: when some cards on the board have already been revealed and the first card flipped does not match any previously inspected card, the player may intentionally choose an inconsequential second card to avoid disclosing additional information to the opponent.
In this context, the player faces two potentially conflicting objectives-either to maximize the probability of winning the game or to maximize the expected point gain.
These differing objectives can lead to distinct optimal strategies, thereby introducing variability and potential noise into data analysis and interpretation.
On the other hand, the solitaire version of the matching-pairs game reduces the objective to a single optimal strategy: clearing the board with the minimum number of moves.

This version is cleaner in that it relies more directly on the player's ability to memorize the experimental stimuli and their positions with fewer interfering factors and therefore constitutes a more suitable tool for cognitive experimentation.
In developing an auditory version of Memory, a pair refers to two audio stimuli that are defined as belonging together, constituting the ground-truth identity for scoring.
Conceptually, three types of pairs are possible: (1) original-original, (2) original-manipulated, and (3) manipulatedmanipulated.
The first type serves as the classic baseline, in which two identical, unmodified items form a pair.
Experimental effects arise, in principle, from comparisons between this baseline and the latter two types.
In the original-manipulated condition, participants must match an original item with a manipulated version of itself-a match based on perceptual similarity.

Because the manipulated stimulus preserves only part of the information present in the original, successful matching requires listeners to rely on induced auditory representations to establish correspondence.

By contrast, the manipulated-manipulated condition collapses back into identical matching: two items subjected to the same manipulation can be matched purely on acoustic features, without engaging the intended auditory-memory processes.

For these reasons, the latter condition does not constitute a meaningful test of perceptual processing within the paradigm, and we therefore restricted the design to the first two pairing types (i.e., identical and similarity-based matching).

The use of music as the experimental stimuli poses two primary challenges: (1) because music unfolds over time, the auditory cards cannot be played simultaneously; and (2) unlike the original Memory game-where the images themselves indicate which cards are being viewed-the auditory version requires additional visual cues to signal which card is currently active.
To implement the audio-visual mapping, we incorporated a color change on the selected card along with an equalizer-style animation to indicate that audio is being played (see Figure 1).

text.text: Furthermore, when the cursor hovers over a card, it exhibits a subtle rotation, suggesting that it is about to be turned over.

These dynamic visual elements serve to reinforce the connection between auditory perception and spatial card identity, thereby preserving the playability of the original game while maintaining clarity in an auditory context.
Additionally, we designed a three-click structure to promote interactional consistency, enhancing clarity and strengthening participants' sense of agency, thereby increasing engagement.
The three-click system was developed to operate at the level of a turn-the basic unit of gameplay in which the player flips two cards and receives feedback.
The player clicks on a first card, triggering a flipping animation, a color change, and playback of the associated audio.
An equalizer-style animation is displayed during sound playback.
Second click: Upon selection of the second card, the audio playback and animation of the first card are interrupted, while its color state persists to indicate that it has been selected.
The second card then undergoes the same visual sequence: flip animation, color change, and equalizer animation.
Once the second click occurs, the outcome of this turn is determined, and the feedback animations differ depending on whether the two match.
When the two cards do not match, both execute a lateral shake animation to signal the error.
For correct matches, the cards display a pulsating scale animation (zooming in and out), providing positive reinforcement.
The score is updated the moment the second card is clicked.
As the second card plays, players can immediately hear whether it matches the first card, and the score update provides instant confirmation of their listening result.
Third click: Playback of the second card is interrupted, and its animation stops.
This serves as the settlement action, updating the game board based on the result of the turn.
If the two selected cards form a matching auditory pair, they are removed from the board.
If not, both cards show a shaking animation and are flipped back, and all visual indicators of these two cards are reset.
The interaction structure is designed to always play the sound of the currently selected card, interrupting any ongoing playback of the previously selected card.

Consequently, clicking the first card initiates its audio, clicking the second card stops the first and plays the second, and the third click at any position stops the second as the game proceeds to the next turn.
This design allows participants to decide how long they would like to listen to each sound, supporting self-paced processing and enhancing their sense of agency during the task.

By integrating animation indicators, animation feedback, score feedback, and a consistent three-click turn system, every piece of feedback triggered by the player's interaction with the system aligns with their listening experience throughout the game, thereby ensuring an intuitive user experience in TuneTwins by linking feedback to action.
To provide natural and intuitive feedback during gameplay, we implemented a surface scoring rule displayed to participants throughout the game.

Under this rule, participants receive +20 points for a memorized match (i.e., a match in which the second card was previously observed), +10 points for a lucky match (i.e., a match made by chance, without prior observation of the second card), 0 points for a non-match between two newly revealed cards, and -10 points for a mismatch (i.e., an incorrect pairing of a previously observed second card).
The rationale is that lucky matches, although they do not involve memory-related cognitive processing, remain technically successful matches.

Presenting them as entirely unrewarded would likely confuse participants; assigning a positive but reduced reward (+10) relative to memorized matches (+20) preserves the intuitive logic of the game while implicitly incentivizing memory-based decisions.
For performance evaluation and data analysis, the system permits a separate analytical scoring rule.
For example, the current study applied the analytical rule of assigning +1 point for memorized matches, 0 points for both nonmatches and lucky matches, and -1 point for mismatches.
Because lucky matches do not reflect memory-based cognitive processing, they receive 0 points under this scheme, equivalent to nonmatches.
The analytical rule thus isolates genuine memory performance from chance-based successes, yielding a cleaner metric for evaluating the cognitive demands of the task.

Beyond the specific configuration used in the present experiment, the dual-layer scoring framework provides methodological flexibility by allowing the surface scoring rule and the analytical rule to be adjusted independently of each other, depending on the research objectives.

text.text: In game design theory, the progress of a game relies on player interaction, where agency is exercised through their choices and actions.
Although uncertainty is often viewed as limiting player agency by reducing a clear sense of control or choice, it is paradoxically this very unpredictability that makes decisions feel consequential.
From an experiment design perspective, the game must also be sufficiently challenging to avoid ceiling effects and to capture meaningful individual differences in performance.
At the same time, it should not be so difficult or frustrating that players are discouraged from completing it.

Ultimately, calibrating the tension between too much and too little freedom-that is, creating constraints that provide enough challenge without overwhelming the player-remains a fundamental principle of game design (Salen Tekinbaş & Zimmerman, 2003).

text.text: We conducted two simulation studies representing extreme performance boundaries, generated from two contrasting gameplay strategies: a chance strategy and an optimal strategy.
The chance strategy is characterized by random card selection throughout the game, representing performance in the absence of memory or strategic behavior.
The optimal strategy is characterized by perfect memory retention, in which the player encodes each card's position upon its first reveal and subsequently pairs all cards without error.
Performance was quantified as the number of turns required to clear the board.
We expected real-world participants' performance to fall within these theoretical bounds.

text.text: In our first, proof-of-concept experiment, we examined whether pitch information is indispensable for music recognition.
Because this study targeted a predominantly Western audience, we compiled a corpus of 48 instrumental theme tunes drawn from popular television programs.

text.text: The two versions of each track represented two levels of degradation: in the first level, pitch cues remained partially perceptible (moderate degradation), whereas in the second level, pitch information was no longer perceivable (severe degradation).
A pilot study (n = 10) confirmed the perceptual difference between the two degradation levels.
We expected that reducing or eliminating perceivable pitch cues would impair participants' ability to memorize the music excerpts, leading to more errors in the game.
A total of 367 participants completed 576 games, yielding 12,679 judgments.
Participants reported their gender as women (n = 149), men (n = 187), and non-binary or undisclosed (n = 31).

We received data from participants in 54 countries, with the largest groups coming from the United States (n = 86), the Netherlands (n = 56), Germany (n = 32), the United Kingdom (n = 32), and Spain (n = 29).

We report the data collected thus far, as this study is ongoing.
To evaluate whether the game encourages sustained engagement, we examined how many times participants completed the game.
Specifically, we calculated the number and proportion of participants who finished at least once, as well as those who played at least two, at least three, and at least ten games.

text.text: In the Congo hunter-gatherer sample, we invited 48 BaYaka participants to play the game individually.
Of those, 71% of participants continued playing after completing the first game, and 63% of participants played ten or more games.
Participants were informed that they were free to stop at any point, and two exercised this option by requesting to discontinue after only a few rounds.

In contrast, many individuals voluntarily approached the experimenter outside of scheduled testing sessions to request additional play, and some even requested to play TuneTwins in place of other planned experiments.

This pattern indicates not only that the task instructions were intuitive-participants were able to understand how to play the game solely through observationbut also that the game itself was genuinely engaging for this group.
A similar pattern was observed at the NEMO Science Museum.
With a strict 15-minute time limit per participant, including the introduction, completing ten games was not feasible.
Nevertheless, all invited participants finished at least one game, and the vast majority completed at least three games despite the time constraint.

In this paper, we introduced the conceptualization and design process of TuneTwins-a matching-pairs gamified experimental paradigm for music cognition research and demonstrated its potential as a reliable, engaging, and scalable experimental tool.

Using data collected from diverse populations-including a hunter-gatherer community in Congo, Dutch museum visitors, and online participants from 65 countries-we showed that the task elicits meaningful behavioral variation and that many participants voluntarily continue playing.
These findings underscore the paradigm's practical value for collecting data on musical memory performance.

The proof-of-concept experiment indicated that the paradigm is sensitive to systematic differences in auditory processing demands introduced by pitch degradation, supporting its usefulness as a behavioral measure of auditory memory performance.
Game scores showed a clear monotonic decline as degradation increased, with effect sizes ranging from moderate to very large.
At the same time, performance in this paradigm is likely shaped by multiple sources of variance beyond auditory degradation alone.

These may include individual differences in cognitive ability, variation in the perceptual difficulty of specific stimuli, positional biases on the game board, and learning effects across repeated play.
Such factors may be particularly relevant for understanding the greater variability observed at higher levels of degradation.
Future work should model these influences more explicitly across successive games in order to better isolate the contribution of auditory memory to performance.
As Table 1 illustrates, engagement patterns varied markedly across data-collection contexts.

text.text: In the Congo field study, where BaYaka participants played face-to-face with the experimenter, 34 of 48 individuals (71%) continued beyond the first game, and 30 (63%) completed ten games (two rounds of the five levels)-with several participants voluntarily requesting additional sessions.
At the NEMO Science Museum, where a 15-minute time limit constrained participation, all 174 participants completed at least one game and 145 (83%) completed three or more.

The global online deployment, by contrast, relied on fully unsupervised participation: of 2,623 registered players, 1,628 (62%) completed at least one game, 834 (32%) at least two, 582 (22%) at least three, and 149 (6%) persisted through all eleven levels despite encountering randomized difficulty ordering.

This gradient from supervised to unsupervised settings mirrors a well-documented pattern in online research: participants in web-based studies face considerably less situational demand than those in laboratory settings (Hoerger, 2010), resulting in consistently higher attrition rates.

text.text: As with any voluntary online study, participants who persevere to advanced levels may differ systematically from those who disengage earlier.
This is a common challenge in unsupervised web-based data collection and should be taken into account when interpreting performance at advanced levels.
Notably, in designs that compare a larger number of conditions or require finer-grained contrasts, greater amounts of data will naturally be needed.
In the global online deployment, condition assignment was counterbalanced such that each difficulty level was represented approximately evenly across the participant pool.
Under this design, the critical requirement is not that participants complete all levels, but that sufficient numbers of games are obtained.
In addition, each completed game contributed multiple card-pairing trials as individual observations.
As the proof-of-concept data illustrate (see Figure 4), each game often involved at least 16 trials, and typically more because mismatches generated additional turns before completion.

text.text: TuneTwins is highly adaptable and can be configured to address a wide range of research questions in musical memory and auditory cognition.

The board size is inherently scalable: although we used an 8-pair (4×4) configuration on the grounds that it offers an optimal balance between discriminability and cognitive load, simpler or more complex versions can be created by adjusting the number of cards.
Scoring rules can likewise be modified depending on the construct of interestfor example, by assigning different weights to memory errors, response speed, or strategic choices.
Stimulus assignment is fully flexible.

While the proof-of-concept experiment used Western television theme tunes pre-screened for recognizability among a predominantly Western audience, researchers can substitute culturally appropriate material without altering the game mechanics.

Boards may employ different types of musical materials (e.g., familiar melodies to probe long-term memory, or unfamiliar melodies to examine working memory) and can be tailored to test sensitivity to specific musical dimensions.
Multiple manipulation levels may be mixed within a single board to estimate effect sizes, or isolated across separate boards to maintain tighter experimental control.

The current implementation also records fine-grained behavioral data-including click timestamps, card locations, memory states, match types, and scoring dynamics-enabling detailed modeling of individual strategies and differences across conditions.

Although the present study used a randomized order of difficulty levels, future designs may introduce structured progressions (e.g., easy-to-hard) to sustain motivation while controlling for learning effects.
Moreover, our current version remains close to the traditional matching-pairs format to preserve intuitiveness.
A consequence of the design choice is that the ground truth of each pair-whether two cards belong together as identical or similar items-is predetermined by the experimenter.
Future versions could relax this constraint and explore designs in which pair relationships are determined by participants' behavior rather than being imposed in advance.
In sum, TuneTwins offers an engaging, intuitive, and reliable framework for studying musical memory and auditory cognition.

Its flexible structure allows researchers to tailor task difficulty, stimulus type, scoring rules, and representational demands, making it suitable for investigating a wide range of cognitive processes-including memory, perception, learning, similarity judgments, and cross-cultural auditory cognition.

The combination of adaptable stimulus design, precise behavioral logging, and principled computational modeling renders the paradigm a promising alternative to existing methods in music cognition research.

As an open-source and extensible project within the Amsterdam Music Lab's MUSCLE framework (https://github.com/Amsterdam-Music-Lab/MUSCLE; Janssen et al., 2023), it provides a robust foundation for developing new experimental manipulations and for advancing our understanding of how humans perceive, remember, and interact with music.

text.text: Moreover, evidence from three distinct deployment contextsan indigenous hunter-gatherer community, a public science museum, and a large-scale online study-demonstrates that the game's intuitive design and engaging gamified structure successfully sustain participant motivation across repeated play, time constraints, multiple difficulty levels, and culturally diverse populations.

This makes TuneTwins well suited for citizen science research (Hilton, 2024; Honing, 2021), which offers an attractive means of addressing sampling bias while capturing the individual variability-ultimately contributing to a more nuanced and generalizable understanding of music cognition.

text.text: Collectively, these features position TuneTwins as a versatile and forward-looking paradigm for future research in music psychology and cognitive science.
